review: 1:4 סוֹד הַחֲסִידוּת — 1 Tim 3:16 μυστήριον τῆς εὐσεβείας; the Hebrew keeps סוֹד in its Danielic sense of a revealed secret (Dan 2:18, 27) with חֲסִידוּת for εὐσέβεια, rather than a descriptive phrase like 'the teaching of godliness'.

2:1 הַמָּשִׁיחַ אֲדֹנֵינוּ — the Arabic أَنْتَ الْمَسِيحُ رَبُّنَا is an explicit 'You are'; the Hebrew keeps a verbless equational clause (the pattern of 1 Kings 18:39, יְהוָה הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים) because the addressee is already established in stanza 1 and the shorter line matches the tune. Both nouns are definite, so this is apposition, not a construct chain.

2:2 פִּסְחֵנוּ הַיָּחִיד — 1 Cor 5:7 (כִּי־פִסְחֵנוּ אַף־הַמָּשִׁיחַ נִזְבַּח); the singular 'our Passover' is kept, and הַיָּחִיד carries the Arabic الْوَحِيد without turning it into 'only' as an adverb.
2:4 רֹאשֵׁנוּ הַנִּכְבָּד — Eph 1:22 (רֹאשׁ לַכֹּל); the Hebrew keeps רֹאשׁ as headship rather than 'leader', so the stanza ends on the resurrection's gift to the church.
3:3–4 וַתֹּאמֶר: זֹאת עֲשׂוּ … לִזְכֹּר — Luke 22:19; the colon is the glossary's rule for direct speech, and לִזְכֹּר keeps the infinitive of the memorial command rather than a noun.
5:4 בַּחֲתֻנָּה וּבַמַּלְכוּת — Rev 19:7 (כִּי־בָאָה חֲתֻנַּת הַשֶּׂה) with Rev 11:15; the two nouns are kept apart so the stanza names both the wedding and the reign, not a vague 'glory'.
